intro: Most of the Bible tells a story or gives a law. This unit turns to the books that sing and the books that argue. The Psalms are 150 poems that have been sung in synagogues and churches for more than two thousand years. The wisdom books, Proverbs, Job, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs, ask plain questions: How should I live? Why do good people suffer? Does anything last? What is love?

You will read these books closely, in translation. You will learn how Hebrew poetry works, with its paired lines and its pictures from daily life. You will sort the psalms by type, meet an Egyptian text that resembles Proverbs, follow the argument in Job to the storm at its end, and see why Jewish and Christian readers have read a love poem as something more.

By the end you will be able to name the pattern in a Hebrew poem, tell a lament from a hymn, explain how different traditions have used these texts, and write a psalm-shaped poem of your own. Everything here is the study of a text and its readers. Nobody is asked to believe or disbelieve; everyone is asked to read carefully.
bigQuestion: What happens when a tradition keeps poems and arguments that do not agree, and keeps singing them?

chapters.title: The Psalms: Praise, Lament, Thanks
chapters.bigQuestion: How can one collection of ancient poems still give words to so many different feelings and communities?

story.title: One Psalm, Two Rooms
story.kicker: The same words are sung in Hebrew on Friday night and in English on Sunday morning, and each room hears them a little differently.
paragraphs: It is Friday evening on the North Side of Chicago. The sun is going down, and a synagogue is filling up. A cantor stands at the front and begins to sing in Hebrew. The words are old. They come from the Book of Psalms, the songbook of the Hebrew Bible. Some people sway. Some read along in a prayer book that prints the Hebrew on one side and English on the other.

The service that welcomes the Sabbath uses several psalms in a row. One of them, Psalm 95, opens with a call to sing. Another, Psalm 29, describes a storm rolling over the sea and the mountains. The people in the room have heard these poems every week of their lives. For many of them, the sound of the Hebrew matters as much as the meaning.

Two days later, a few miles away, a church choir stands up on Sunday morning. The organ plays a few bars. Then the choir sings in English: "The Lord is my shepherd." That is Psalm 23. Some people in the pews know it by heart. A few whisper the lines along with the choir. Others simply listen.

Both rooms are singing from the same book. Jewish tradition calls it Tehillim, which means "praises." Christians call it the Psalms, from a Greek word for a song played on a stringed instrument. The Hebrew words were written more than two thousand years ago. The English words came much later, through many translations.

In this chapter you will read some of these poems closely. You will see how they are built, what kinds there are, and why so many singers, from ancient priests to Chicago gospel choirs, have kept coming back to them.
story.think: Why might a poem written thousands of years ago still be sung every week in two different religious communities?

lessons.title: One Hundred Fifty Poems
lessons.mainIdea: The Book of Psalms is a collection of 150 poems, arranged in five smaller books.
reading: Open a Bible to the middle and you will probably land in the Book of *Psalms*. It is the longest book in the Bible by chapters. There are 150 psalms. Each one is a separate poem. Some are only a few lines long. Psalm 117 has two verses. Psalm 119 has 176 verses and is the longest chapter in the Bible.

The psalms are not in random order. Ancient editors arranged them in five smaller *books*. Each book ends with a short line of praise called a *doxology*. Jewish tradition has long noticed that five books of psalms match the five books of the Torah. Many scholars think the editors meant that match on purpose.

Where did the psalms come from? The text itself does not say when each one was written. Many scholars think the poems were composed over several centuries. Some may go back to the time of the kings, before 586 BCE. Others clearly speak from the time after the exile to Babylon. The collection as we have it was probably finished a few centuries before the Common Era.

In Jewish tradition the book is called Tehillim, "praises." That name fits many psalms but not all. Some psalms are full of complaint and sorrow. As you read, remember that this is an anthology, a gathered collection. It holds many voices, moods and moments from ancient Israel's life.

words.d: the book of 150 Hebrew poems in the Bible; Jewish tradition calls it Tehillim, meaning praises
a short line of praise that closes a section; each of the five books of Psalms ends with one
in the Psalms, the five smaller collections the editors used to arrange the 150 poems

lessons.title: Names at the Top
lessons.mainIdea: Many psalms carry a heading naming David or another figure, and readers disagree about what those headings mean.
reading: Most psalms begin with a short heading, often printed in smaller type. Scholars call it a *superscription*. It may name a person, an instrument, a tune or an occasion. Seventy-three psalms carry the Hebrew words "le-David," which most English Bibles print as "A Psalm of David." Others name Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon or Moses.

What does "of David" mean? The Hebrew word le can mean "by," "for" or "belonging to." Jewish and Christian tradition long read it as "written by David," the shepherd who became king. The books of Samuel describe David as a musician who played the harp. Many scholars today think some headings were added later by editors. They read "of David" as "in David's collection" or "in David's style."

A few headings tell a story. Psalm 51's heading connects it to the moment when the prophet Nathan confronted David about Bathsheba. Psalm 3 is linked to David fleeing from his son Absalom. These headings invite the reader to hear the poem as a scene from David's life. Whether they record history or a later reading, they shape how the psalm is heard.

Some headings are musical notes we no longer fully understand. The word *Selah* appears seventy-one times in the Psalms. It may have marked a pause or a change in the music. Nobody today is certain. When you meet these words, treat them as clues about how the psalms were once performed.

words.d: the heading above a psalm, which may name a person, a tune, an instrument or an occasion
a Hebrew word in many psalms, probably a musical or performance note; its exact meaning is not known

look.title: Two Ways to Read a Heading
look.text: Psalm 3 opens with the heading "A Psalm of David, when he fled from Absalom his son." A reader in a traditional synagogue or church may hear the poem as David's own prayer on that night. A reader in a university class may say: the heading was added by an editor to connect an older poem to a famous story. Both readers are looking at the same seven words.
look.prompt: What does each reader gain from their way of reading? Does the poem change meaning if the heading was added later?

check.q: About how many psalms carry David's name in their heading?
check.why: Seventy-three psalms have the heading le-David. Asaph is named on 12, and Moses on only 1.

check.q: Why do some scholars read "of David" as "in David's collection" instead of "written by David"?
choices: The Hebrew word le can mean by, for or belonging to.
The psalms are all about kings.
The word David does not appear in Hebrew.
check.why: The Hebrew preposition le has several meanings, so the heading is open to more than one reading.

check.q: What is Selah most likely?
choices: The name of a Hebrew king
A note about music or a pause
check.why: Selah appears in many psalms and is probably a performance note. Its exact meaning is not known.

lessons.title: Kinds of Psalms
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars sort the psalms into types, such as praise, lament, thanksgiving, royal, wisdom and pilgrimage, by their shape and purpose.
reading: Read a few psalms in a row and you will notice patterns. Some shout with joy. Some cry out in pain. In the early 1900s a German scholar named Hermann Gunkel sorted the psalms by their shape and their setting in life. His categories, with some changes, are still used today. Learning them helps you see what a psalm is doing.

A *praise* psalm, or hymn, calls people to praise God and gives reasons. Psalm 100 and Psalm 150 are examples. A *lament* is a cry for help. It names a trouble, asks for rescue and often ends with trust. Laments are the largest group. Psalm 13 begins, "How long?" A *thanksgiving* psalm looks back on a rescue and says thank you, as in Psalm 30.

Other types are tied to a setting. A *royal* psalm is about the king, such as Psalm 2 or Psalm 72. A *wisdom* psalm teaches, like a page from Proverbs. Psalm 1 and Psalm 37 fit here. Psalms 120 to 134 each carry the heading "A Song of Ascents." Many scholars think pilgrims sang them on the way up to Jerusalem for festivals.

The types are tools, not walls. Many psalms mix them. Psalm 22 begins as a lament and ends as praise. When you read a psalm, ask what it is doing: calling for praise, crying for help, saying thanks, teaching or walking a road. Then look for the turn, the moment where the mood shifts.

a psalm type that cries out in trouble, asks for help and often ends in trust; the largest group
a psalm type that looks back on a rescue and gives thanks
a psalm type centered on the king of Israel

lessons.title: Psalm 23: The Shepherd
lessons.mainIdea: Psalm 23 builds its comfort out of two pictures, a shepherd and a host, and the parallel lines that carry them.
reading: Psalm 23 is the best-known poem in the Bible. It is only six verses long. It opens with a picture: "The LORD is my shepherd." In the ancient Near East, kings were often called shepherds of their people. Here the speaker makes the picture personal. The one who guides is *my* shepherd, and the speaker is one sheep in the flock.

The poem moves through a landscape. There are green pastures and still waters. Then comes a dark valley. The King James Version calls it "the valley of the shadow of death." The Jewish Publication Society Tanakh of 1917 uses the same phrase. Some modern translations render it "the darkest valley." The Hebrew word can mean deep darkness. Both readings are defensible.

Halfway through, the picture changes. The shepherd becomes a host. A table is set, the guest's head is anointed with oil, the cup overflows. In the last verse the speaker hopes to dwell "in the house of the LORD." Jewish readers have often heard this as the Temple. Many Christian readers hear it as heaven. The text itself does not explain.

Notice the *parallelism*. Hebrew poetry rarely rhymes. Instead, it says a thing and then says it again in a new way. "He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters." The second line matches the first and adds a new image. This is the basic music of the psalms.

words.d: the main pattern of Hebrew poetry: a line is followed by a second line that repeats, sharpens or answers it
one who guides and protects a flock; in the ancient Near East, a common image for a king or a god

look.title: Psalm 23, Verse 4
look.text: Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.
look.prompt: Find the two halves of this verse. What does the second half add to the first? Why might a shepherd's rod and staff be a comfort to a sheep?

check.q: Which two pictures does Psalm 23 use for God?
check.why: Psalm 23 begins with a shepherd guiding a flock and ends with a host setting a table.

check.q: What is parallelism?
choices: Saying a thing, then saying it again in a new way
Repeating one word at the start of every line
check.why: Parallelism is the second line matching and adding to the first. Hebrew poetry rarely rhymes.

check.q: How have Jewish and many Christian readers differed on "the house of the LORD" in the last verse?
choices: Jewish readers say a palace; Christians say a tent.
Jewish readers say a synagogue; Christians say a church.
Jewish readers say it is a mistake; Christians say it is correct.
Jewish readers have often heard the Temple; many Christians hear heaven.
check.why: The text does not explain the phrase. Jewish readers have often read it as the Temple; many Christian readers read it as heaven.

lessons.title: Psalm 1: Two Roads
lessons.mainIdea: Psalm 1 opens the whole book by contrasting two ways of life, and its first word is translated differently in Jewish and Christian Bibles.
reading: Psalm 1 stands at the door of the book. Many scholars think editors placed it there as an introduction. It is a *wisdom* psalm. It does not pray or praise. It teaches. It sets two kinds of people side by side: the one who delights in God's *Torah*, or teaching, and the wicked who do not.

The first Hebrew word is ashrei. The King James Version of 1611 translates it "Blessed." The Jewish Publication Society Tanakh of 1917 translates it "Happy." Both are fair. The Hebrew word describes a person whose life is going well, someone you might envy. That is why some translators avoid "blessed," which can sound like a blessing from above.

The psalm works by *contrast*. The good person is like a tree planted by streams of water. Its leaf does not wither. The wicked are like chaff, the dry husks the wind blows away at harvest time. A tree is rooted and lasting. Chaff is light and gone in a moment. The two images carry the whole argument.

Because Psalm 1 comes first, some readers say it tells you how to read the rest. The psalms, on this view, are meant to be studied like Torah, not only sung. Others point out that most psalms are prayers, not lessons. Either way, the editors chose to start the songbook with a teaching.

words.d: Hebrew for teaching or instruction; the first five books of the Bible, and more broadly God's teaching
setting two things side by side to show how different they are; Psalm 1 contrasts the tree and the chaff
a psalm type that teaches how to live, much like the Book of Proverbs

look.title: Blessed or Happy?
look.text: Psalm 1 begins with the Hebrew word ashrei. The King James Version (1611) reads: "Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly." The Jewish Publication Society Tanakh (1917) opens the same verse with "Happy is the man." Both translate the same Hebrew word. "Blessed" can suggest a gift from God. "Happy" describes how the person's life is going.
look.prompt: Which word would you choose, and why? How does the choice change the feel of the whole psalm?

check.q: What kind of psalm is Psalm 1?
choices: a lament that cries for help
a royal psalm about the king
check.why: Psalm 1 teaches by contrasting two ways of life, which makes it a wisdom psalm.

check.q: How does the JPS 1917 Tanakh translate the first word of Psalm 1?
check.why: JPS 1917 reads "Happy is the man." The King James Version reads "Blessed." Both translate the Hebrew ashrei.

check.q: In Psalm 1, the wicked are compared to what?
check.why: The good person is a rooted tree; the wicked are chaff, the dry husks the wind blows away.

lessons.title: Psalm 137: Songs in Exile
lessons.mainIdea: Psalm 137 is a lament from the Babylonian exile that ends with a cry for revenge, and readers have long wrestled with that ending.
reading: In 586 BCE the Babylonian army destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple. Many people of Judah were taken to Babylon. Psalm 137 speaks from that time. It begins: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion." *Zion* is a name for Jerusalem and its Temple hill. The singers have hung up their harps.

The captors ask for a song. The psalm answers with a question: "How shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land?" Then the speaker makes a vow. If I forget Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill. Let my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth. The poem turns grief into a promise to remember.

The last verses are hard to read. The speaker calls down a curse on Babylon and on Edom, a neighbor that helped in Jerusalem's fall. The final verse blesses the one who smashes Babylon's infants against the rock. This is a cry for revenge from a people who saw their own city burned. The psalm does not soften it.

Readers have handled this ending in many ways. Some synagogues and churches leave the last verses out when the psalm is sung. Some readers say the poem is honest: it shows rage as a real human feeling brought before God. Others read it as a warning about where hatred leads. The chapter's job is to see what the text says and to notice how readers respond.

words.d: a name for Jerusalem, especially the hill of the Temple; used in the Psalms for the city and its people
being forced to live away from your homeland; the Judeans' years in Babylon after 586 BCE

look.title: Psalm 137, Verses 1 and 4
look.text: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. … How shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land?

check.q: Psalm 137 speaks from which moment in history?
choices: The building of the Temple by Solomon
The wandering in the wilderness after Egypt
The exile in Babylon after 586 BCE
check.why: The psalm names the rivers of Babylon and remembers Zion, which fits the exile after Jerusalem fell in 586 BCE.

check.q: What does Zion mean in the Psalms?
check.why: Zion is a name for Jerusalem, especially the Temple hill. Babylon and Edom are the enemies in Psalm 137.

check.q: How have some communities handled the last verses of Psalm 137?

They moved them to the start of the psalm.

check.why: Some synagogues and churches omit the closing curse when singing the psalm; others keep it and read it as honest grief.

lessons.title: Psalm 150: Every Instrument
lessons.mainIdea: Psalm 150 closes the book with a burst of praise that names instrument after instrument.
reading: The Book of Psalms ends with five psalms that each begin and end with *Hallelujah*, Hebrew for "praise the LORD." Psalm 150 is the last. It is short, only six verses. It gives no story, no complaint and no argument. It is pure call to praise. Many scholars see it as the closing doxology for the whole book.

The psalm is built on one command, "praise," repeated more than ten times. First it says where: in the sanctuary and in the heavens. Then it says why: for mighty acts and greatness. Then it says how, with a list of instruments. The trumpet, the harp and lyre, the tambourine and dance, strings and pipe, loud cymbals, clashing cymbals.

The instruments were the orchestra of the Temple in Jerusalem. The books of Chronicles describe Levite musicians playing cymbals, harps and lyres during worship. Psalm 150 reads like a roll call of that orchestra. The tambourine and dance may point to celebration outside the Temple, in the streets and villages.

The last verse widens the circle. "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." Not only priests, not only Israel, but everything that breathes. Then one final Hallelujah. Many readers have noticed the shape: the book that began with one person studying Torah in Psalm 1 ends with all creation making noise.

words.d: Hebrew for praise the LORD; it opens and closes each of Psalms 146 to 150
a holy place set apart for worship; in the Psalms, usually the Temple in Jerusalem

look.title: Psalm 150, Verse 6
look.text: Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Praise ye the LORD.
look.prompt: Who is invited to praise in this verse? How is that different from the earlier verses, which name a place and a list of instruments?

check.q: What does Hallelujah mean?
check.why: Hallelujah is Hebrew for "praise the LORD." It frames the last five psalms.

check.q: Psalm 150 answers where, why and how to praise. What is the "how"?
check.why: The how is a roll call of instruments: trumpet, harp, lyre, tambourine, strings, pipe and cymbals.

check.q: Which biblical books describe Levite musicians playing in the Temple?
check.why: The books of Chronicles describe Levites playing cymbals, harps and lyres in Temple worship.

lessons.title: In the Synagogue
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish worship has used the psalms daily, weekly and at festivals for well over two thousand years.
reading: The psalms began as songs, and Jewish communities never stopped singing them. The *synagogue* is the Jewish house of prayer and study. There, psalms fill the daily service. A morning service includes a group of psalms of praise called Pesukei d'Zimra, "verses of song." Psalm 145 is recited three times a day in traditional practice.

Each day of the week has its own psalm. The Mishnah is a Jewish law code written down c. 200 CE. It records that the Levites sang a set psalm each day in the Temple. Psalm 24 on Sunday, Psalm 92 on the Sabbath, and so on. Many synagogues still say the psalm of the day. It is a living link to the Temple that fell in 70 CE.

On Friday evening the service that welcomes the Sabbath, Kabbalat Shabbat, uses Psalms 95 to 99 and Psalm 29. Jewish mystics in the town of Safed put this order together in the 1500s. At festivals such as Passover, Jews sing the *Hallel*. That is Psalms 113 to 118, a set of praise psalms. Christian readers note that the Gospels describe Jesus and his disciples singing a hymn after the Passover meal.

Psalms also mark hard times. Traditional Jewish mourners recite Psalm 49 or Psalm 16 in a house of mourning. Psalm 23 is often said at funerals. In many communities people gather to recite the whole book of Psalms for someone who is sick. For these readers the psalms are less a text to study than a voice to borrow.

words.d: a Jewish house of prayer and study
Psalms 113 to 118, a set of praise psalms sung at Jewish festivals such as Passover
the collection of Jewish oral law written down c. 200 CE; it records which psalm the Levites sang each day

look.title: A Psalm for Each Day
look.text: The Mishnah (Tamid 7:4) lists the psalm the Levites sang in the Temple on each day of the week: Sunday Psalm 24, Monday Psalm 48, Tuesday Psalm 82, Wednesday Psalm 94, Thursday Psalm 81, Friday Psalm 93, Sabbath Psalm 92. Psalm 92's own heading reads "A Psalm, a Song for the Sabbath day." Many synagogues still recite these psalms today.

check.q: What is the Hallel?
check.why: The Hallel is the set of praise psalms 113–118 sung at Passover and other festivals.

check.q: Which Jewish text records the psalm the Levites sang on each day in the Temple?

lessons.title: In the Church
lessons.mainIdea: Christians took the psalms into their worship from the beginning, chanting, translating and setting them to new music.
reading: The first Christians were Jews who already knew the psalms. The New Testament quotes the Psalms more than any other book of the Hebrew Bible. Christian tradition reads many psalms as pointing to Jesus. Psalm 22, which begins "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?", is quoted in the Gospels at the crucifixion. Jewish readers read the same psalm as a lament of an individual or of Israel.

Monks in the Middle Ages sang the whole book every week. They used *Gregorian chant*, a plain, unaccompanied melody in Latin. The chant is named for Pope Gregory I, who died in 604 CE, though the music was written down centuries later. In many Catholic and Orthodox churches, chanted psalms are still the backbone of daily prayer.

The Protestant Reformation of the 1500s changed the sound. Reformers in Geneva wanted everyone, not just monks, to sing. They turned the psalms into rhymed verses in French, the Genevan Psalter of 1562. English Puritans did the same. The first book printed in British North America was the Bay Psalm Book, in 1640 in Massachusetts.

Psalms also shaped larger music. Composers set psalm texts in Latin, German and English. Handel's Messiah of 1742 draws on the Psalms among other books. Later, African American spirituals borrowed psalm images of rivers, exile and deliverance. Psalm 137's "rivers of Babylon" became a reggae hit in the 1970s.

a book of psalms arranged for singing or prayer, such as the Genevan Psalter of 1562

lessons.title: Gospel Music in Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's Black churches turned psalm-shaped praise into gospel music in the 1930s.
reading: In the 1920s and 1930s, hundreds of thousands of African Americans moved north to Chicago in the Great Migration. They brought their churches with them. In those churches a new music was born. It mixed the blues, spirituals and hymns. People called it *gospel*.

Thomas A. Dorsey is often called the father of gospel music. He had been a blues pianist. After a personal tragedy in 1932, he wrote "Take My Hand, Precious Lord." He led the choir at Pilgrim Baptist Church on Chicago's South Side for decades. Mahalia Jackson, who sang in Chicago churches, carried gospel to the world.

Gospel songs are not psalms. But they share the psalms' shapes. A gospel song often begins in trouble and ends in trust, like a lament. Many are built on repeated praise, like Psalm 150. Singers use *call and response*: a leader sings a line, and the choir answers. Some scholars compare this to the parallel lines of Hebrew poetry.

Chicago's gospel story shows something about the psalms. Their forms travel. A shepherd in Judah, a monk in Latin, a farmer in Geneva and a choir on the South Side have all used the same moves: praise, cry, thanks, and a turn from one to the other.

lessons.title: How the Lines Work
lessons.mainIdea: Parallelism comes in several patterns, and spotting them is the first step to writing a psalm-shaped poem.
reading: In 1753 an English bishop named Robert Lowth gave a set of lectures on Hebrew poetry. He gave *parallelism* its name and sorted it into kinds. His labels are still taught. The first kind is *synonymous*: the second line says the first line again in new words. "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork" (Psalm 19:1, KJV).

The second kind is *antithetic*: the second line says the opposite. Psalm 1 ends this way. The LORD knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish. Proverbs is full of this pattern. The third kind Lowth called synthetic: the second line simply carries the first forward, adding a step or a result.

Later scholars added a warning. The second line rarely just repeats. It usually sharpens, narrows or raises the stakes. "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?" (Psalm 13:1, KJV). Forgetting is bad. Hiding a face is worse. Reading the second line as "more," not "again," unlocks the poem.

Psalms also use *imagery*, pictures drawn from daily life. A shepherd, a tree, chaff, a fortress, a cup, a storm. And some use an *acrostic*, where each line or section begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Psalm 119 has 22 sections of 8 verses, one for each letter. The pattern disappears in translation, but a good footnote will tell you it is there.

a kind of parallelism where the second line states the opposite of the first

lessons.title: Your Own Psalm
lessons.mainIdea: You can write a psalm-shaped poem by choosing a type, using parallel lines and imagery, and building a turn.
reading: This lesson is a workshop. Your task is to write a short poem in the shape of a psalm. You do not need to share the beliefs of the psalmists to do this. Poets of every faith and none have borrowed the form. Your poem can be addressed to anyone or anything: a friend, a city, the wind, an idea.

Step one: choose a type. Praise, lament or thanks. If praise, decide what you are praising and why. If lament, name a real trouble, ask for help and plan your turn to trust or hope. If thanks, look back on a rescue and say who or what got you through. Step two: pick two images from your own life, the way the psalms use shepherds and trees.

Step three: write in pairs of lines. Say it, then say it again with more. Try at least one antithetic pair, where the second line says the opposite. Do not rhyme. Step four: build a *turn*, a moment where the mood shifts. In laments the turn often comes with the word "but." In praise, the turn may be the widening circle, as in Psalm 150.

Step five: give it a heading, like a real superscription. It can name a tune, an instrument or an occasion. Then read it aloud. The psalms were made for the voice. If you are working in a group, try call and response. One reads the first line of each pair, and the rest answer with the second.

words.d: the moment in a poem where the mood or direction shifts, for example from complaint to trust
a lesson where you make something and then look at it together

chapters.bigQuestion: Why does the Bible keep books that answer the question "how should I live?" in such different ways?

story.title: Seven Days of Silence
story.kicker: Three friends travel to sit with a man who has lost everything, and the moment they open their mouths, things go wrong.
paragraphs: The Book of Job opens with a rich man in a land called Uz. He has seven sons, three daughters, thousands of animals and many servants. The text says he is blameless and upright. Then, in one day, messengers arrive one after another. Raiders took the oxen. Fire took the sheep. A wind knocked down a house, and all ten children were inside. Job tears his robe and falls to the ground.

Soon after, sores cover his body from head to foot. He sits down in the ashes and scrapes himself with a broken piece of pottery. His wife tells him to curse God and die. He refuses. Three friends hear the news and come from far away: Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar. When they see him from a distance, they do not recognize him. They weep and throw dust in the air.

Then they do the wisest thing in the whole book. They sit on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights, and nobody says a word. The text says they saw that his grief was very great. Jewish tradition later drew a rule from this scene: when you visit a mourner, wait for the mourner to speak first.

On the eighth day Job speaks, and curses the day he was born. Now the friends answer, and the trouble begins. Eliphaz says, gently at first, that the innocent do not perish. Bildad says God does not twist justice, so Job's children must have sinned. Zophar says Job is getting less than he deserves. Each speech says the same thing: suffering must be earned.

Job refuses that answer. He knows he did nothing to deserve this. For nearly thirty chapters the four men argue in poetry. The friends defend the rule that the good prosper and the wicked fall. Job demands to face God in court. At the end, a voice speaks from a storm. It does not answer the way anyone expected. This chapter follows that argument and the other books that join it.
story.think: Why might sitting in silence have been wiser than anything the three friends said afterward?

lessons.title: What Wisdom Writing Is
lessons.mainIdea: Wisdom literature is a genre found across the ancient Near East that asks how to live well, based on experience rather than law or prophecy.
reading: Most of the Hebrew Bible tells Israel's story or gives its laws or records its prophets. A few books do something else. They ask a plain human question: how should a person live? Scholars call these books *wisdom literature*. In the Hebrew Bible they are Proverbs, Job and Ecclesiastes. Many readers add the Song of Songs and some psalms.

Wisdom books have a distinct voice. They rarely mention Moses, the covenant at Sinai or the exodus from Egypt. They do not say "thus says the LORD" the way prophets do. Instead they observe. They watch ants, lazy people, kings, farmers and fools, and they draw lessons. Their authority comes from experience, not from a vision.

This kind of writing was not unique to Israel. Egypt produced instruction books for young officials for more than a thousand years. Mesopotamia had proverb collections and a poem about a righteous sufferer. In the Bible, 1 Kings 4 says Solomon's wisdom was greater than that of "all the children of the east country" and of Egypt. The comparison itself shows that the writers knew of other nations' wisdom.

In Jewish tradition Proverbs, Job and Ecclesiastes sit in the third part of the Tanakh, the *Ketuvim* or Writings. In Christian Bibles they sit together after the history books, along with Psalms and the Song of Songs. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles add two more wisdom books, Sirach and the Wisdom of Solomon. Protestant Bibles place those in the Apocrypha or leave them out.

Hebrew for Writings, the third section of the Tanakh, where the wisdom books are placed

lessons.title: Egypt's Amenemope
lessons.mainIdea: An Egyptian instruction book, the Instruction of Amenemope, closely resembles a section of Proverbs, and scholars debate how the two are related.
reading: In 1888 the British Museum acquired an Egyptian papyrus. It held a text called the *Instruction of Amenemope*. An official named Amenemope writes advice to his son in thirty chapters. Scholars date the work to roughly the late second millennium BCE, perhaps c. 1100 BCE, though the copy is later. In 1923 the text was published, and readers of the Bible noticed something.

Proverbs 22:17 to 24:22 is a section that begins with a call to hear "the words of the wise." Its sayings often match Amenemope's, in order and in image. Both warn against moving a boundary stone. Both say riches can fly away like a bird. Proverbs 22:20 even seems to mention "thirty" sayings, though the Hebrew word is hard to read. Most scholars think the Hebrew writer knew the Egyptian text, or a version of it.

Not everyone agrees on the direction. A few early scholars argued the Egyptian text borrowed from Hebrew. Most today think the borrowing went from Egypt into Proverbs, because Amenemope is older and the Egyptian genre is much older still. Some suggest both drew on a shared pool of sayings. The debate is about literary history, not about which text is true.

What does this mean for reading Proverbs? For many scholars it shows that Israel's wisdom teachers were part of an international conversation. For many religious readers it shows that wisdom can be found among all peoples, a point Proverbs itself makes. Both readings can note the differences too. Proverbs speaks of the LORD, Israel's God, where Amenemope speaks of the Egyptian gods.

lessons.title: The Two-Line Saying
lessons.mainIdea: A proverb packs a lesson into two parallel lines, often by contrast, and is meant to be memorized and tested against life.
reading: The Book of *Proverbs* is a collection of collections. Its headings name Solomon, "the men of Hezekiah," Agur and King Lemuel. Chapters 1 to 9 are long speeches from a father to a son. Chapters 10 to 29 are hundreds of short sayings. The book does not tell a story. It is more like a pantry, stocked with sayings to take down when you need them.

The basic unit is the two-line saying. Most proverbs in the middle chapters are *antithetic*: the second line says the opposite of the first. "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger" (Proverbs 15:1, KJV). The contrast makes the saying easy to remember and hard to argue with.

Proverbs also uses pictures. A gold ring in a pig's snout. A door turning on its hinges. A city with no walls. Some sayings use numbers: "there be three things … yea, four" (Proverbs 30:18, KJV). Some are riddles that take a moment to decode. All of them are short enough to carry in your head.

Notice that proverbs describe what usually happens, not what always happens. "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it" (Proverbs 22:6, KJV). Most readers treat this as a general truth, not a guarantee. That gap between "usually" and "always" is exactly where the Book of Job will push.

words.d: a biblical book of wise sayings and speeches, mostly short two-line proverbs, with headings naming Solomon and others
a kind of parallelism where the second line states the opposite of the first
a short, memorable saying that states a lesson drawn from experience

lessons.title: The Fear of the LORD
lessons.mainIdea: Proverbs makes "the fear of the LORD" the starting point of wisdom, and readers debate what kind of fear it means.
reading: Proverbs 1:7 is often called the motto of the book: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge." The phrase comes back again and again. Proverbs 9:10 repeats it with "wisdom" in place of knowledge. Job 28:28 and Psalm 111:10 say nearly the same thing. For the wisdom writers, this is where learning starts.

What is *the fear of the LORD*? The Hebrew word yirah can mean terror, but it can also mean awe and deep respect. Many Jewish and Christian teachers have read it as reverence: knowing that you are not the center of the universe. Some scholars note that in Proverbs it usually appears beside words like humility, honesty and turning from evil.

The idea does a job in the book. Proverbs is confident that a person can learn how life works by watching it. But it does not want the student to become proud. The fear of the LORD puts a limit on human cleverness. As one saying puts it, there is no wisdom or counsel against the LORD (Proverbs 21:30).

In Proverbs 1 to 9, wisdom is personified as a woman. *Lady Wisdom* calls out in the streets and invites people to her house. Proverbs 8 says she was with God before creation. Jewish readers have often linked her to the Torah. Some early Christian writers linked her to Christ. Both readings go beyond what the text itself states, and each community says so in its own way.

lessons.title: The Woman of Valor
lessons.mainIdea: Proverbs ends with an acrostic poem praising a capable woman, which Jewish families sing on Friday night.
reading: Proverbs closes with a poem, Proverbs 31:10 to 31. In Hebrew it is an *acrostic*: its twenty-two verses begin with the twenty-two letters of the alphabet in order. It describes a woman the King James Version calls "a virtuous woman." The Hebrew is eshet chayil. Chayil can mean strength, worth, wealth or valor. Many translators now write "a woman of valor."

The poem is a portrait of work. The woman buys a field and plants a vineyard. She spins wool and flax, trades with merchants, makes and sells linen. She gives to the poor. Her lamp does not go out at night. Her husband is known at the city gate, where business and law took place, and her children call her blessed.

In Jewish homes this poem has a special place. Many families sing or recite Eshet Chayil at the table on Friday night as the Sabbath begins. Traditionally a husband sings it to his wife. Some read it as praise of the actual woman of the house. Some medieval Jewish readers understood it as praise of the Sabbath itself, or of the Torah, or of wisdom.

Readers today discuss the poem from many angles. Some point out that it praises a woman for her skill, judgment and business sense, not only her beauty. "Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain" (Proverbs 31:30, KJV). Others note that the poem is spoken by a man about a woman and reflects an ancient household. Both observations are about the same text.

words.d: a poem whose lines or sections begin with the letters of the alphabet in order; Proverbs 31:10–31 is one

lessons.title: Who Wrote Proverbs?
lessons.mainIdea: Proverbs names several sources in its headings, and tradition and scholarship read those names in different ways.
reading: The first verse of the book says, "The proverbs of Solomon the son of David, king of Israel." Jewish and Christian tradition long held that Solomon wrote the book. First Kings 4:32 says he spoke three thousand proverbs. The Talmud, in tractate Bava Batra, discusses who wrote down Proverbs and other books. It names Hezekiah and his circle.

The book's own headings name more than one source. Proverbs 10:1 begins a second Solomon collection. Proverbs 22:17 introduces "the words of the wise." Proverbs 25:1 says the men of King Hezekiah, who ruled c. 715 to 686 BCE, copied out more Solomon sayings. Proverbs 30 is "the words of Agur," and Proverbs 31 "the words of king Lemuel," taught by his mother.

Most scholars today read these headings as signs of a long editing process. Sayings from many centuries and sources, some from Egypt, were gathered under Solomon's famous name. This is common in the ancient world, where a great figure's name often stood over a whole genre. Traditional readers may accept Solomon as the author while granting later editing. The headings themselves leave room for both.

Why does it matter? The question of authorship changes how you read a saying. If it is Solomon's, it comes with a royal stamp. If it is an anonymous teacher's, it stands or falls on whether it is true to life. Proverbs itself seems more interested in the second test. It keeps asking the reader to look and see.

words.d: a title line inside a book, such as "the words of Agur," that names a section's source
the great collection of Jewish law and discussion completed c. 500 CE; it discusses who wrote the biblical books

lessons.title: The Wager in Heaven
lessons.mainIdea: Job's prose opening sets up a test that Job never learns about, and it raises the question the whole book argues.
reading: The Book of *Job* is built like a sandwich. Chapters 1 and 2 and the end of chapter 42 are prose, a simple story. Everything in between is poetry. The story opens in Uz, a land the text does not locate. Job is not called an Israelite. Many scholars think the story is meant to feel like a folktale from anywhere.

The scene shifts to heaven. God praises Job's goodness before a court of heavenly beings. One of them, called in Hebrew *ha-satan*, "the adversary" or "the accuser," asks a question. Does Job fear God for nothing? Take away his rewards and he will curse you. God allows the test. Job loses his wealth, his children and his health. He does not curse God.

Readers should be careful with the name. In Job the adversary is a member of God's court, a kind of prosecutor. He is not yet the devil of later Jewish and Christian tradition. Most scholars say that fuller picture developed after Job was written. Translations that print "Satan" as a name can hide this.

The wager creates a gap in knowledge. The reader knows why Job suffers. Job does not, and never finds out. His friends do not know either, though they think they do. That gap drives the book. Every speech that follows is an attempt to explain suffering by people who lack the one fact the reader has.

words.d: a biblical book about a good man who loses everything and argues with his friends and with God about why
Hebrew for the adversary or accuser; in Job, a member of God's court who proposes the test
ordinary written language, not poetry; Job's opening and ending are prose

look.title: Does Job Fear God for Nothing?
look.text: The adversary's question in Job 1:9 can be paraphrased: Is Job good for free, or is he good because it pays? Take away the pay and see. The question is not only about Job. It asks whether anyone can be good without a reward. The book tests the question by removing every reward Job has.
look.prompt: Restate the adversary's question in your own words. Is it a fair question? What would count as an answer?

check.why: Job 1–2 and the end of chapter 42 are prose; the long middle is poetry.

choices: A member of God's court who acts as accuser

choices: That he is in the land of Uz
That his suffering began as a test
check.why: The prose opening shows the reader the wager; Job and his friends argue without that fact.

lessons.title: The Friends' Theology
lessons.mainIdea: Job's friends defend the belief that suffering is always deserved, and the book shows that belief failing against Job's case.
reading: Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar each take turns speaking, and Job answers each one. This goes around three times, from chapter 3 to chapter 31. Scholars call the friends' shared belief *retribution theology*. The idea is simple. God rewards the good and punishes the wicked in this life. So if you are suffering, you must have done wrong.

The friends are not villains. Their belief comes straight from Proverbs and Deuteronomy, where obedience brings blessing. Eliphaz begins kindly. He reminds Job how he once comforted others. But as Job keeps insisting he is innocent, the friends grow harsh. By chapter 22 Eliphaz is inventing crimes: you took a poor man's clothing, you sent widows away empty.

Job's answers grow bolder. He agrees that God is powerful. He denies that God is being fair to him. He wants a trial, a chance to argue his case in court. "Oh that I knew where I might find him!" (Job 23:3, KJV). In chapter 31 he swears a long oath of innocence, listing sin after sin he did not commit. Then the text says the words of Job are ended.

A fourth speaker, Elihu, appears in chapters 32 to 37. He is younger and angry at everyone. Many scholars think his speeches were added later, since nobody answers him and he is not mentioned at the end. Whether original or added, Elihu shows that the argument had not been settled. The question of undeserved suffering stays open.

words.d: the belief that God rewards the good and punishes the wicked in this life, so suffering must be deserved
the fourth, younger speaker in Job 32–37, whose speeches many scholars think were added later

look.title: Bildad's Logic
look.text: In Job 8, Bildad argues (in paraphrase): God does not twist justice. Your children sinned, and God punished them. If you are pure, God will restore you. Ask the older generation; they will tell you the same. Job answers (in paraphrase): I know all that, but how can a person win a case against God? He destroys the blameless and the wicked alike.

The belief that God does not exist
The belief that all people will be rewarded after death

check.why: Retribution theology holds that God rewards good and punishes evil in this life, so the sufferer must have sinned.

lessons.title: The Voice from the Storm
lessons.mainIdea: God answers Job out of a whirlwind with questions about creation, not with an explanation, and readers disagree about what that answer means.
reading: In chapter 38 the argument stops. "Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind." What follows is two long poems of questions. Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Have you entered the storehouses of the snow? Can you bind the stars? Who feeds the lion and the raven? The poems tour the whole creation: sea, dawn, weather, wild animals.

Two creatures get the longest treatment. *Behemoth*, a huge land animal, and *Leviathan*, a sea creature that breathes fire and laughs at spears. Some readers see the hippopotamus and the crocodile. Others see mythic monsters of chaos, like those in other ancient Near Eastern texts. Either way, they are wild, untamed and not made for humans.

Notice what the speech does not do. It never mentions the wager. It never says Job sinned. It never explains suffering. Job answers briefly. He says he spoke of things he did not understand, and he repents "in dust and ashes" (Job 42:6, KJV). The Hebrew of that verse is famously hard, and translations differ on whether Job gives up, is comforted or changes his mind.

Readers have drawn very different lessons. Some say the speech means humans cannot understand God's plan and should trust. Some say it shows a world that is vast and wild and not built around human justice. Some say Job is being silenced by power. Then comes the prose ending: God says the friends spoke wrongly and Job spoke rightly, and Job's fortunes are restored. Readers argue about that ending too.

words.d: the storm from which God speaks to Job in chapters 38 to 41
a great sea creature described in Job 41; read as a crocodile by some and as a mythic chaos monster by others
a huge land animal described in Job 40; often identified with the hippopotamus

lessons.title: Vanity of Vanities
lessons.mainIdea: Ecclesiastes questions whether anything lasts, and its key word hevel has been translated many ways.
reading: The book opens with a voice called Qohelet in Hebrew. The word probably means one who gathers an assembly. The Greek translators rendered it *Ecclesiastes*, and the King James Version calls him "the Preacher." The speaker says he was king in Jerusalem, and tradition identified him with Solomon. Most scholars date the book much later, c. 300 BCE, partly because of its late Hebrew and its Persian loanwords.

The book's key word is *hevel*. It appears about thirty-eight times. Literally it means breath, vapor or mist. The King James Version translates it "vanity." Modern translators have tried "futility," "meaningless," "absurd" and "mere breath." Each choice changes the book's mood. Vapor is real but cannot be held. That is Qohelet's picture of human effort.

Qohelet watches the sun rise and set, rivers run to the sea, and generations come and go. Nothing changes. "There is no new thing under the sun" (Ecclesiastes 1:9, KJV). He tries wisdom, pleasure, work and wealth, and finds that death takes the wise and the foolish alike. This is a direct challenge to the confidence of Proverbs.

Yet Ecclesiastes is not simply gloomy. Again and again the speaker says: eat your bread with joy, enjoy your work, enjoy life with the one you love. The famous poem in chapter 3 says there is a time for everything. A time to be born and to die, to weep and to laugh. In Jewish tradition the book is read at the festival of Sukkot, a season of joy. The last verses tell the reader to fear God and keep the commandments. Many scholars think an editor added them.

words.d: a biblical book of a speaker called Qohelet, or the Preacher, who asks whether anything under the sun lasts
Hebrew for breath, vapor or mist; the key word of Ecclesiastes, translated vanity in the King James Version
the Hebrew name of the speaker in Ecclesiastes, probably meaning one who gathers an assembly

lessons.title: The Song of Songs
lessons.mainIdea: The Song of Songs is love poetry between two voices, and Jewish and Christian traditions have long read it as an allegory as well.
reading: The *Song of Songs* is eight chapters of love poetry. Two main voices speak, a woman and a man, with a chorus called the daughters of Jerusalem. They praise each other's bodies with images from the land: gazelles, vineyards, doves, spices, a garden. The woman speaks more than the man. God is never clearly named in the book.

The title means "the best of songs." The first verse links it to Solomon, and tradition called him its author. Many scholars think it is a collection of love poems from different times, put together after the exile. Some compare it to Egyptian love songs. Its frank celebration of desire made some ancient readers ask why it belonged in scripture.

The answer, for both Jews and Christians, was *allegory*, reading a story as a picture of something else. Rabbi Akiva, c. 100 CE, is quoted in the Mishnah defending the book strongly, calling it the holy of holies among the Writings. Jewish tradition read the Song as the love between God and Israel. It is read in synagogues at Passover, the festival of Israel's freedom.

Christian readers from Origen in the third century to Bernard of Clairvaux in the twelfth read it as the love between Christ and the church, or Christ and the soul. Since the 1800s, many scholars and religious readers have returned to reading it as human love poetry. Some hold both readings at once. The text supports the plain reading; the traditions supply the second.

words.d: a biblical book of love poems between a woman and a man, also called the Song of Solomon or Canticles

lessons.title: Three Books That Disagree
lessons.mainIdea: Proverbs, Job and Ecclesiastes give different answers to the same question, and the Bible keeps all three.
reading: Put the three main wisdom books side by side and they argue. Proverbs says the world runs on order: work hard, act justly, fear the LORD, and things will go well. Job says: I did all that, and look at me. Ecclesiastes says: the wise and the foolish both die, so enjoy what you have while you have it.

Some readers try to smooth this out. They say Proverbs gives general rules, Job the exceptions and Ecclesiastes the limits. Others think the disagreement is the point. Jewish tradition preserved debates between rabbis without settling them, and some scholars see the same habit in these books. A *canon* that keeps disagreeing voices invites its readers to think.

The three books also share a lot. All three prize honesty over easy comfort. All three watch the world closely. All three, in their final forms, come back to the fear of God: Proverbs at its start, Job at its center in chapter 28, Ecclesiastes in its last verses. Whether that shared ending came from the authors or from editors is one of the debates.

For a student in a public school, the wisdom books offer a model of how a tradition thinks. They show that ancient readers asked the hard questions too. Why do good people suffer? Does anything last? What is love? The Bible's answer was not one book but four, kept together and left in tension.

words.d: the list of books a community counts as its scripture; the biblical canon keeps Proverbs, Job and Ecclesiastes together
